messages.subject: Field ID of Whales
messages.body_plain:
Dear Listmembers,
I am aware this question might be slightly off-topic, but perhaps somebody
using ship-based distance sampling on the Balaenopteridae whales can give
me a hint on useful ID literature. I am interested in ID features for
field conditions (great distance, bad light, ...) and remember having seen
comparisons with regard to time interval between blow and emerging of the
dorsal fin and the fluke. Is such data available printed or at www ?
How useful are such features - is there considerable variation with
respect to size, age or sex ? I'd welcome any hints.
Thanks and greetings
Wilken

messages.subject: Pooling question - a summary
messages.body_plain:
Question:

> >I am unsure what is the best way to pool my data, I have line transect data

>from annual game counts over several years, with repetitions, and through

> >diverse vegetation types. Any advice would be very helpful....

> >My data set:

> >7 years (with 8-16 repetitions per year) of data of observations of 14

> >ungulate species along 8 line-transects through various amounts of 11

> >vegetation types.

> >I wish to find the long-term average density of each species per vegetation

> >type.

> >Firstly, I have analysed the data by pooling all the transects for all the

> >years and repetitions and stratifying for vegetation types. This gives me a

> >nice number of observations, to work out the density estimate per vegetation

> >type, and gives me the overall average density across the years, (which is

> >what I am interested in). However, I now realize the sample size is 1, and

> >so my variance is inaccurate - right?

> >Reply:

> >I'll ignore the species -- you can either have them all in one project file
> >with
> >a species field in the observation layer and use data selection in the data
> >filter to select each one, one by one, or you could have a separate project
> >file
> >for each species (in which case the Template option in project setup will be
> >useful to you - look up Template in the online help index).

> >Seems to me you want to try detection function pooled across all habitats,
> >separate detection functions for each habitat type and detection function as
> >a
> >covariate.  We'd like to set up a project to allow you to try all 3, and get
> >valid density estimates for each case.  Seems that you are not interested in
> >by-
> >year estimates, so we'll pool over years.

> >How about the following:
> >You have a stratum layer with one record for each veg type
> >You have a sample layer with one record for each transect within each veg
> >type.
> >The transect length is the length of transect in that veg type mutiplied by
> >the
> >number of times it was surveyed (e.g., surveyed 7 times in 7 years then
> >multiply
> >by 49).
> >You have an observation layer with one record for each observation.  Pool
> >observations across years and repeats within years as we're not interested
> >in
> >these.

> >Then try an analysis with detection function global, another with detection
> >function by stratum and a third with the stratum label (ie veg type) as a
> >factor
> >covariate.  See what AIC tells you (assuming no other problems with the
> >data),
> >but I would tend to err on the side of the higher-parameter model as you're
> >most
> >intersted in the by stratum estimates of density (ie density by habitat
> >type),
> >rather than the global density estimate; it's the latter that AIC is
> >designed to
> >give you the best bias-variance trade off on.

> >There is one problem with this analysis -- Distance thinks that the
> >transects
> >within each stratum are independent, but in fact they are not.  Will only be
> >a
> >problem if you want to compare the densities among habitats to judge
> >statistical
> >significance of the difference/estimate confidence intervals on differences,
> >etc.  You could do this with a bootstrap, where you bootstrap by transect
> >(ie 1-
> >8) and when you select a particular transect, the relevent parts of the
> >transect
> >are put under each habitat stratum.  You'd have to program this outside of
> >Distance (calling Distance to do the analysis) -- one of these days I'll get
> >around to adding such a facility within the program (it's also useful for
> >trend
> >analysis, where you repeat transcts across years).  This non-independence
> >would
> >not be a big problem if you had lots of transects, but with only 8 it may
> >cause
> >quite a covariance in estimates between veg types.  Can't say without trying
> >it.

> >END

messages.subject: Re: Error message - writing to data file
messages.subject_clean: Error message - writing to data file
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julian, list,

The data selection criteria are applied to each record one by one.  What you are
asking Distance for in your query

(Label = "9") and (Label = "8") and (Label = "7")

is to select records where *all* of the following are true: the Label field has
a value "7" *and* the Label field has a value "8" *and* the Label field has a
value "9".  Since for any individual record only one of these can be true at
once, there are no records selected.  What you want is the criterion

(Label = "9") OR (Label = "8") OR (Label = "7")

or, more concicely, you could have

Label IN ("7","8","9")

or

Label BETWEEN "7" AND "9"

The numbers have to be in quotes because Label is a text field.  For this reason
I'd be a bit careful with the BETWEEN operator, as selecting regions 9-12 with
Label BETWEEN "9" AND "12" won't work.  The text character that is larger than
"9" is "0", and after that comes "A", "B", "C", etc!  So probably better to
stick with the IN operator.

When setting up a data filter, it's a good idea to check that it is doing the
right thing by having a look at what data is selected.  You can do this by
ticking the box "Echo data to log" under Tools | Preferences | Analysis.  The
log will then list the data after the INFILE command, and the previous command
FIELDS will give you a clue as to which field is which.  Once you are sure the
data filter is working the way you want, you should turn the "Echo data" switch
back off to save your project getting too large.  Another way to achieve the
same thing is to have Distance save the data and command files to a temp
directory, where you can examine the data file and check it looks right.  To do
this, tick on "Debug mode".

Lastly, I thought the error message

Found selection criterion: {SELECT * FROM [lyrRegion] WHERE (Label = "9") and
(Label = "8") and (Label = "7")}
** Error: Encountered a problem while writing to the data file 'C:\DOCUME~1
\Leo\LOCALS~1\Temp\dst9F.tmp'  **

was rather cryptic, so I've changed the code so that in future under these
circumstances it will say

Found selection criterion: {SELECT * FROM [lyrRegion] WHERE (Label = "9") and
(Label = "8") and (Label = "7")}

** Error: The following data selection criterion creates a query with no
records.  Please check the text of the criterion. {SELECT * FROM [lyrRegion]

WHERE (Label = "9") and (Label = "8") and (Label = "7")}  **

Cheers,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk

messages.body_plain:
I am in the process of analysing some bird data gathered using the line
transect method. I have previously used Distance 3.5, but now using 4.1
release 2. I am currently finding the error message "Encountered a problem
while executing the data creating query" when attempting to post-stratify
by species in the observation layer (Model definition).

I had also had another problem [as described by Julian Easton (4th Aug
04)], but have found that was simply a problem of syntax in defining the
criteria in the data filter. I suspect the above problem is similar but
have as yet failed to find a solution.

The area in question is an area of forest of three distinct vegetation
types, split into about ten coupes (destined for logging in various ways)
and some controls. Unfortunately both coupes and controls and sometimes
transects within coupes and controls are across veg boundaries. The data I
am dealing with currently is all pre-logging data, and hence the main
interest is in establishing some baseline bird-density data in the
different veg types, but will also need to deduce densities within the
coupes and, I hope, by species - at least the of more common ones.

In Distance 3.5 I was able to post-stratify to species level and would like
to be able to do the same in 4.1 without creating a different project for
each species.

Thanks in anticipation of the answer...

Paul Lefort

messages.subject: Re: ActiveX, internal error 429
messages.body_plain:
Hi Todd,

(I'm cc'ing this to the list so it's in the archives for others)

Since you say that Distance worked fine for months, it must be that you are
encountering something Microsoft calls "DLL Hell" -- that is when some application
you have installed replaces a shared file (dll or other shared file) with either
(a) an older version of the same file (which install scripts should never do in
theory but sometimes do in practice), or (b) a newer version which has a bug in it
or breaks backward compatibility (again, should never happen in theory!).  Quite
often, the problems are caused by Microsoft's own products!

Since the Open dialog shows on your screen, the source of the error is not likely
the common control dll.  Also, the error message gives the error source as D4Util,
which is my utilities dll.  I've had a look at my code ShowCommonDialog, and the
only D4Util routines that are called from there after you click "Open" is code to
extract the directory name from the file you chose to open.  This code in turn uses
Microsoft Windows Script.  So my guess is that your version of the Script engine
has been corrupted somehow.  You don't say what version of Windows you're using but
I would guess it's Windows 2000 as that's the only version for which I can't bundle
scripting in with the Distance setup, for technical reasons.  (I also can't bundle
it in with XP or Longhorn, but it shouldn't get corrupted on those systems.)  In
any case, go to
http://www.microsoft.com/scripting
and download the appropriate version of Microsoft Windows Script 5.6 (or whatever
the latest version is) for your operating system and language.  Install it, reboot,
and see if that fixes the problem.

In any case, please contact me off the list to say how you get on.  If it works,
I'll add the fix to the list of known problems and solutions.

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re:
messages.body_plain:
Are you saying that you want it to predict a non-zero density even
though nothing was seen because by chance (especially with p=.1) you may
miss animals that were there? If you ask Distance to construct estimates
by sample it does so solely based on the observations and the predicted
p. You should really be thinking about the average density as the
predicted value for a single point sample.  The density by sample was
included for the unusual situation in which a sample was something like
a replicate from the entire area (eg different  replicate surveys).
Using the mean density is all it can do unless you move into the realm
of spatial models.  A simple spatial model is a regional stratification.
  Imagine 2 strata with 10 sample points each. The predicted density for
the 10 points in stratum 1 is the average density in that stratum and
likewise for stratum 2.  Now imagine further sub-dividing the strata.
If you did so such that each point was in its own strata, what would you
estimate to be the density in the strata with no observations?  If you
strictly used stratification they would have to be assigned 0 density.
However you could imagine fitting a smooth surface to the density
predictions, in which case the predicted density for areas with sample
points with 0 observations would be the "smoothed average" of
neighboring areas and thus it could be non-zero.  Spatial modelling can
be done oustide of Distance and will eventually be added to Distance.

Hope this helps.  --jeff

messages.subject: Kangaroo project
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have just commenced a study on eastern grey kangaroos in a water
catchment area near Sydney. One of my main questions relates to their
dung, and I need to correlate actual roo density from Distance sampling
with dung density also from Distance sampling for a range of habitats to
model their relative distribution in the catchment (their dung is
important for parasites and like deer easier to see in dense veg).
Therefore, I am essentially pre-stratifying according to habitat near
the water. Now here is my problem:

-In some of these habitats you can easily see the dung but not many
kangaroos. However, the one or two kangaroos that you may see you do so
with great difficulty. Would you:

1) Sample more of this type of habitat so that the encounter rate
increases and variance can adequately be estimated OR
2) I am open for more suggestions

The open areas of my study site are covered in kangaroos and dung so it
quite easy to do. In this instance would you run shorter transects and
more of them and in contrast in the dense areas described above run
longer transects and more of them. The length of the transects in these
dense habitats, or even all habitats, will of course be governed by how
large each remnant is. How would effort be stratified?

I am really looking forward to some suggestions

Kindest
regards
Michael

Department of Biological Sciences
Macquarie University

Mobile: 0414 50 70 80

messages.subject: Re: Kangaroo project
messages.body_plain:
Michael,

Just a few comments (and then some) regarding the questions you posed:

1.  I recommend you review the following paper because it is probably
one of the best papers addressing (most of)the assumptions of using dung
surveys to monitor abundance:

Title: Estimating deer abundance from line transect surveys of dung:
sika deer in southern Scotland
Author(s): Marques FFC, Buckland ST, Goffin D, Dixon CE, Borchers DL,
Mayle BA, Peace AJ
Source: JOURNAL OF APPLIED ECOLOGY 38 (2): 349-363 APR 2001

2.  Many of your questions are related more to basic sampling design
issues than issues specific to distance sampling.  I would recommend you
confer with a statistician.  The rule of thumb is that you want to apply
more effort to areas with greater densities of roos (or dung) because
you would expect more variability in density estimates in those areas.

3.  One question that came to mind in reading your post is that if you
are interested in the density of dung because of parasites why is it
necessary to correlate roo density with dung density?  Why not simply
estimate dung density?

4.  I have some experience using distance sampling to estimate density
of white-tailed deer pellet groups (dung).  If roos are similar I would
recommend more transects distributed across your study area (rather than
fewer long transects).  Finding dung is not hard (you can get many
'sightings' within a short distance) so estimating the detection
function is less problematic than accounting for the variability in the
encounter rate among transects.  Hence, more transects means a better
estimate of variability among transects.

5.  Related to #3 above, dung density is related to the density of roos
when they deposit the dung - that is, there is a temporal component you
need to consider.  For example, most dung surveys for white-tailed deer
are conducted in the spring before spring vegetation emerges and the
dung has been deposited over the winter period when little decomposition
occurs.  Thus, the distribution of dung reflects the distribution of
deer during winter - not at other times of the year.  I don't know if
this is an issue for roos, but something you should consider if
inferences about habitat use is of importance.

6.  It sounds like your habitat characteristics vary widely across the
study area - you should assume that detection functions differ among
habitats and design your study accordingly.  In even the best of
conditions I found observers missed about 50% of pellet groups at 3 feet
(~1 m) from the transect line.  Likewise, not all observers have the
same detection function - and with all the dung observations you will
likely collect for each observer it is not difficult to detect these
differences!

7.  I have found that the 'survival' of dung depends on habitat type.
In deciduous forests dung disappears faster (a deeper litter layer) than
in coniferous habitats.  I am sure it varies seasonally as well.

8.  Detection of dung on the transect line (g(0)) is <1.  I have found
that observers (myself included!) missed as much as 20-30% of deer
pellet groups within 12 inches of the transect line.

I'm sure I've raised more issues than provided answers, but good luck in
designing your study.  Hope these comments help.

Regards,

Duane

messages.subject: Re: Survey design in Distance 4.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stuart, list,

I'm glad to hear you're using the survey design feature -- I think it's a
wonderful tool, but I agree it takes a bit of work to get things set up.

It sounds to me like there is a problem with the projection of your shape
files.  It's fine to set the geographic coordinate system (GCS) to [None], so
long as you are working with a shapefile where the coordinates are stored in
projected units.  When you set the GCS to [None], Distance simply works with
the x,y coordinates of your shapes and do any reprojecting of them -- so it
works faster.  You need to make sure that the geographic data in your
shapefile is stored in projected units, and that they really are meters if
that is what you have specified.  From your email, it sounds to me like they
may be in kilometers or some other units.  In that case, you can change the
units in File | Properties | Geographic properties.  How you check the
projection depends on the GIS you are using; I'll assume you know how to do
that or have a GIS geek locally who can help you.

Also, check that you are creating the coverage grid as a child of the global
layer, rather than the stratum layer.  To do this, click on the global data
layer in the data layer viewer on the left hand side of the Data tab.  Then
click the "Create data layer" button to create your coverage layer.

If neither of these help, please send me a copy of your project (use File |
Export and save as zip) and I'll see if I can find a problem with it.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Dear List Members:
Although I'm addressing this query to all interested parties, I expect that
it will probably fall to Len to answer; that is, if there is an answer to
the problem.
         I'm designing a survey for kangaroos ( using a helicopter and line
transect sampling) and have taken on the task of using the survey design
facilities in Distance 4.1.  I have created the shape files of the areas to
be surveyed and shape files of the three strata within each of these areas
and, following the instruction in the manual, I can import these files into
Distance.  Where things go awry is when I try to create a coverage grid for
an area.
         The areas I am dealing with range from 14,000 to 18,500 sq.
km.  If I attempt to put in a coverage grid with points 10 km apart, I get
a message the effect that there will be no points in the grid.  If I opt
for the default of points 100 m apart (which you would think is somewhat
ridiculous given the scale at which I am working at), I get a message
telling me that the grid will contain a small number of points
(50-120).  This obviously does not make sense and I suspect that what is
happening is that a 100 m grid is being created for one of the constituent
polygons of the total area.  The geographic properties of the project are
such that the geographic coordinate system is set at [None] and the
shapefile units is set to metres.  Reading Len's reply to a previous query
from a List Member (Barbara, I think), I got the impression that this is
correct.  Am I right?  And, if I'm wrong, is changing the geographic
properties of the project going to solve my immediate problem.
         Any suggestions regarding this will be appreciated.  I hold high
hopes for the idea of being able to use Distance to design surveys, so I am
hoping that my initial attempt at doing so will not founder on what may be
my limited understanding of shapefiles and projections.
Regards,
Stuart

messages.subject: Stratification vs Covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello Len and list!

    I am fairly new to Distance and am currently doing some exploratory
analysis on bird point-count data.  The survey is investigating bird
densities in noisy vs. quiet areas.  I am using Distance as a prelude to
other analyses to decide where to truncate my observations (i.e. at what
distance from the observer is the observation unreliable due to the
noise level).

    The data was collected in six 25m intervals up to 150m from the
observer.  I am currently running half-normal/cosine models with a few
covariates (such as decibel level) after going through a stepwise
covariate-adding process.  However, I also have a few variables that I
feel would be more appropriate for inclusion by post-stratification
rather than as covariates.  These are observer and "treatment vs
control".  When I run models post-stratifying by either of these,
Distance returns the same AIC and other results as if the model was not
stratified at all.  Should I just include them as covariates instead (in
both cases, this returns a lower AIC then the null model)?

Of course, the other option is that I'm totally confused and
stratification has no effect on detection probability!

Thanks very much,
Lucas.

--
Lucas Habib
M.Sc. Candidate
CW405, Biological Sciences Centre
University of Alberta
Edmonton, AB T6G 2E9

Phone: (780) 492-2539

messages.subject: Re: Stratification vs Covariates
messages.body_plain:
Lucas, list:

- Make sure you are selecting detection function by stratum in the Estimate
tab of the Model Definition when you post-stratify - this will give you a
separate detection function in each post-stratum, which is what you want.

- Note that you can only stratify (or post stratify) by one variable at a
time, so you can't test observer and "treatment vs control" at the same time.

- Lastly, note that covariates only affect the scale parameter of the key
function (although they can affect the adjustment terms, depending on what
option you select under Model Definition | Detection Function | Adjustment
terms | Scaling of Distances).  The half normal only has one parameter - the
scale parameter.  So, when you have no adjustment terms, adding a factor
covariate gives the same result as post-stratifying by that factor (both add
one parameter per factor level).  You'll only get a difference when you have
adjustment terms.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
